extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, judges, and inventors interested in patent validity/infringement defenses
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing when prior public use, sale, or disclosure of an invention before patent application will invalidate (abandon) patent rights, and related defenses (breach of confidence, surreptitious patents, statutory modifications such as the Act of 1839).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence in public use forfeits patent right
rubrics_metrics.description: Any acquiescence in the public use, by the inventor, will be an abandonment of his right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention is communicated to the public before a patent is obtained and the inventor voluntarily acquiesces in public use, that acquiescence is evidence that justly forfeits his right. The public, who may have innocently appropriated the invention at expense, should not later be deprived of that use by a delayed assertion of the inventor's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge or presumable knowledge of public use is material
rubrics_metrics.description: The acquiescence of an inventor in the public use of an invention can in no case be presumed when he has no knowledge of such use; but this knowledge may be presumed from the circumstances of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether public use works as a forfeiture depends on whether the inventor knew or should reasonably have known of the public use; this is generally a jury question. If after notice the inventor does not promptly assert his right, such delay is strong evidence of acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent/motive of inventor's acts is material (§303)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention with which the inventor did the acts relied on as proof of 'public use' is material, unless the evidence shows the invention was beyond the inventor's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the inventor used the invention himself, or imparted knowledge to others with or without limitation as to time, extent, or object. Intent to limit use may prevent presumption of dedication; absence of limiting intent supports finding of public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception (§304)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where acts of user were by way of experiment, in order to perfect the invention, the inventor does not lose his right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage by the inventor for experiment or completion—whether public or private—does not prove dedication. The general test: if the evidence stops short of proving use for the purpose of gain, a 'public use' will not be proved. Temporary, limited, or neighborly accommodations for testing do not defeat the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use requires substantiality/unlimited character
rubrics_metrics.description: To defeat a patent it is essential that there should have been a public use of the machine substantially as patented, with the inventor's consent; mere occasional personal experimental use or short limited loans will not take away the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use must be generally allowed or acquiesced in, or at least be unlimited in time, extent, or object. Use without the inventor's consent and adverse to his patent is a clear violation and will not deprive him of his patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale or single transaction may constitute public use (historical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under earlier law a sale to a single person, even a solitary transaction, might amount to a public use or sale with the inventor's consent and thus defeat novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee sold completed machines as articles of commerce for gain (even once), that could be treated as a public use and render the invention not new at the date of the patent. Courts noted this could unfairly extend monopolies and later statutes modified the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1839 — purchaser's prior-use protection and 2-year limit (§307-§309)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act of 1839 provided that persons who purchased or constructed a newly-invented machine prior to the inventor's application shall have the right to use and vend the specific thing without liability; but no patent shall be invalidated by such prior purchase, sale, or use except on proof of abandonment to the public or that such prior use has continued for more than two years prior to application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute enables more safety for pre-application use by individuals. A single prior purchase/sale/use does not per se invalidate a patent unless (a) it amounts to abandonment to the public (shown by circumstances or other evidence) or (b) it continued for over two years before application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular prior act does not automatically prove abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchase, sale, or prior use before application shall not invalidate a patent per se; it must amount to an abandonment to the public, shown by that act together with attendant circumstances or by other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require either additional facts showing public dedication or that the prior use extended beyond two years. Examples: continuous public use with consent, lack of notice, or acts/omissions indicating intent to abandon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arising from breach of confidence does not bar patent if inventor acts promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention has come into public use through a breach of confidence, it cannot be said to be in public use 'with the consent or allowance' of the patentee; only silence after it has become public gives rise to presumption of consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor may entrust confidential knowledge to employees or others; if a recipient fraudulently makes it public, the inventor can obtain a valid patent provided he takes immediate steps to give notice of his exclusive right. Delay or silence risks presumption of acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited permission for accommodation/special purposes does not amount to dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee allows others a limited use of his invention, not for profit but for accommodation, consistent with a clear intention to retain exclusive privilege and the invention not having gotten beyond his control, it will not be a dedication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether evidence excludes that the patentee put the thing into public use for profit. Limited, non-commercial, or controlled uses (including employer-employee contexts where inventor retained control) do not necessarily forfeit rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere delay in applying does not of itself forfeit right absent public use/sale with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere delay to take out a patent, unaccompanied by public use or sale of the thing with the consent or allowance of the patentee before his application, will have no effect upon the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay is only significant insofar as it tends to show acquiescence in public use; without such public acts, lateness alone is not fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory language construed to cover all patentable subject-matter (§309-§310)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Act of 1839 refers to 'machine, manufacture, or composition of matter,' the courts construed 'the invention patented' broadly so the provision embraces whatever is the subject-matter of a valid patent, including processes or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purchaser's protection and the 'specific machine' language are interpreted to mean 'the thing as originally invented' irrespective of whether it is a machine, improvement, or process; this avoids arbitrary distinctions based on terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user protection limited to the specific improvement then invented
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the invention before an application for a patent must be the specific improvement then invented and used by the person who had purchased, constructed, or used the machine to which the invention is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act's object is to protect use of the exact thing purchased/constructed (the specific machine or improvement), not to permit wholesale appropriation of broader inventive concepts beyond the specific article used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreptitious or unjustly obtained patent is a defense (§311)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patentee had surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent for that which was in fact invented or discovered by another, who was using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the same, is a good defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone procures a patent by fraud on the real inventor's rights, the defence is a complete bar to enforcement. One mode is learning the invention from public records or other sources and pirating it; the jury may infer piracy from existence of prior records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior inventor using reasonable diligence can defeat later patent (§312)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two independent inventors exist and one makes earlier application but the other first invented and was using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the thing, the earlier patentee's patent may be defeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defence applies even if the first inventor had not perfected the device, provided he was diligently pursuing adaptation/perfection. Evidence of diligence and prior invention can overcome later formal priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing or patent records put subsequent applicants on inquiry (presumption of knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the real inventor has filed a description at the patent office or obtained a patent, he has given notice to every subsequent applicant; a jury may infer piracy if a later patentee takes out a similar patent, because every subsequent patentee is presumed to have knowledge of prior public records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public records create an evidentiary presumption that later patentees knew of prior disclosures; absence of direct proof of copying does not prevent the jury from inferring surreptitious appropriation.
